description: We are Koyllur Dynamics, a team from UNSA in Arequipa, Peru, led by Dr. Juan Carlos Cutipa Luque and Mechanical and Electronics Engineering students. We combine robotics, design, control, and NASA data to create Rover-Time, an interactive lunar mission simulator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our goal is to inspire young learners to explore STEM, collaborate, and help build Peru’s future in space.
summary:
Rover-Time is a multiuser educational simulator featuring lunar mining missions for junior astronauts. In Peru, PISA 2022 found that only 47% of 15-year-old students reached baseline proficiency in science and 34% in mathematics, highlighting the need to strengthen STEM learning.

Addressing the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge, Rover-Time combines rover exploration, terrain mapping, autonomous route planning, robotic sample collection, and lunar base construction and maintenance.

Using NASA lunar data, physics models, and educational rules, players balance water, oxygen, energy, food, and protection while discovering how their decisions affect mission success. Edu, our AI assistant, provides explanations and tutorials, while multiplayer missions encourage teamwork.

Designed primarily for children aged 7–12, the experience also offers deeper learning opportunities for secondary school, high school, and university students. Our goal is to make engineering trade-offs tangible and develop scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and collaboration.

Next, we will adapt activities by age and evaluate learning with students and teachers through pre- and post-mission assessments. PISA figures describe the educational context, not Rover-Time’s results; its learning impact remains to be measured.
details:
Rover-Time: Lunar Mining Missions for Junior Astronauts

Rover-Time is an interactive educational simulator that enables students to explore the Moon, operate robotic vehicles, and manage a lunar base. It addresses the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge by turning engineering decisions—such as allocating energy, obtaining water, producing food, and maintaining life-support systems—into learning experiences.

Our primary audience is children aged 7–12, with progressively advanced learning opportunities for secondary school, high school, and university students interested in science, engineering, programming, and robotics. We want participants to understand that a mission depends on interconnected systems: difficult terrain affects mobility, expeditions supply the base, and energy availability determines which operations can continue.

What does it do, and how does it work?

Participants select a lunar region and explore an environment built using NASA elevation data and imagery. Elevation data defines the terrain’s shape, while imagery provides its visual appearance. Within this environment, users drive a rover, identify obstacles, plan routes, and collect samples with a robotic arm.

The simulator integrates several activities:

  • Exploration and navigation: Manual driving, virtual LiDAR mapping, and RRT* route planning that considers slopes, obstacles, and vehicle clearance.
  • Robotic manipulation: A six-degree-of-freedom arm uses inverse kinematics and RRT-Connect motion planning to find movements for collecting and transporting samples.
  • Base construction: Placement and connection of habitat, life-support, power, storage, and production modules.
  • Resource management: Management of water, oxygen, hydrogen, food, nutrients, minerals, and energy through educational extraction, processing, and recycling systems.
  • Maintenance and protection: Decisions about repairing and upgrading facilities, with educational events informed by solar activity and particle records.
  • Collaboration: Shared sessions in which participants explore and contribute to a mission.
  • Guided learning: Edu provides tutorials and explanations about the simulator, scientific concepts, and engineering methods.

The experience allows participants to observe consequences and try different approaches. For example, obtaining water from ice requires planning an expedition, collecting and transporting the ice, and allocating energy to process it.

What benefits does it offer?

Rover-Time connects abstract concepts with observable actions. Physics appears in rover movement and stability; mathematics in trajectories and probabilities; chemistry in resource conversion; and programming in control and automation.

The project aims to develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork. Participants can compare alternatives, identify why a decision failed, and adjust their strategies. Teachers can use the simulator to introduce challenges such as selecting a safe route, explaining energy consumption, or maintaining a base with limited resources.

Explanations can follow progressive learning levels: first discovering what happens, then understanding why it happens, and finally exploring the scientific or computational model behind it.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to stimulate interest in STEM and make space exploration more accessible to students with limited opportunities to experience robotics or simulation. Our educational objective is to help learners understand the relationships between terrain, mobility, energy, resources, and the continued operation of a lunar base.

This impact will need to be evaluated through testing with students and teachers. Planned assessment includes comparing understanding before and after gameplay, examining how participants justify their decisions, and observing how independently they solve challenges.

In the longer term, the simulator could evolve into a platform for comparing the performance of different rover types within the same lunar scenario. It could support investigations into how wheels, vehicle geometry, and configurations affect mobility, stability, route completion, and payload transport. More rigorous engineering applications would require model calibration and comparison against physical experiments and specialized simulations.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did we use?

Development involved the main simulator, scientific prototypes, and supporting tools:

  • Game engine and interface: Unity 6, Universal Render Pipeline, Unity Input System, and Unity UI.
  • Programming languages: C# for Unity components and Python for analysis, visualization, geometry, and supporting tools.
  • Scientific and processing libraries: NumPy, Matplotlib, Pandas, Shapely, manifold3d, Pillow, and Requests.
  • Prototyping and scientific visualization: Panda3D, PySide6, Rasterio, and pyproj, alongside the JAXA Earth API in a related Earth–Moon visualization prototype.
  • Browser-based computing: Pyodide, NumPy, and Matplotlib for the scientific viewer.
  • Communication and data: WebSocket, a Cloudflare relay, browser local storage, and JSON and CSV files.
  • Engineering simulation: Ansys Rocky for discrete element method simulations of wheels interacting with granular material.
  • AI assistance: ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex supported programming, debugging, documentation, and educational content development. Groq and Cloudflare support Edu’s conversational service.
  • 3D and audiovisual resources: Custom geometry; models and textures from Poly Haven, ambientCG, and Grab3D; Fictionlab documentation and geometry; NASA Image and Video Library; and FFmpeg.
  • Hardware: Development and analysis computers, with the LEO rover serving as a physical reference for the digital replica.

Our participation in the Laboratorio de Control de Procesos Complejos y Vehículos No Tripulados, located at the Centro de Investigación y Laboratorios Especializados (CIALE), Universidad Nacional de San Agustín de Arequipa (UNSA), in the Engineering Area, provided experience with robotic vehicles. The LEO rover from LIAR–UNSA served as a reference for developing a digital replica and exploring its behavior in challenge scenarios built using NASA data.

What scientific data and references did we use?

The project combines sources with distinct roles:

  • LRO/LOLA, distributed through USGS: Elevation data for constructing lunar terrain.
  • LROC WAC through Moon Trek: Lunar surface imagery.
  • NASA PDS / Lunar Prospector GRS: Regional chemical composition to contextualize resources.
  • NASA CCMC DONKI: Solar energetic particle event records for educational probability models.
  • LRO/CRaTER: Particle counts used to vary an in-game activity index.
  • LCROSS and Moon Mineralogy Mapper, M³: Scientific references concerning lunar water and ice.
  • ESA, JAXA/Nissan, and Fictionlab: Rover design and engineering references.
  • Karaman and Frazzoli; Kuffner and LaValle: References for RRT* and RRT-Connect, respectively.

We distinguish observed data, computational models, and educational rules. For example, CRaTER particle counts do not represent astronaut absorbed radiation doses, and collectible ice quantities are gameplay parameters rather than estimates of recoverable reserves.

What makes the project creative?

Rover-Time was also inspired by research co-authored by our team leader: “Experimental Validation of Translational Single LiDAR 2D Mechanism Into Autonomous Navigation and 3D SLAM of Mobile Robots,” published by IEEE. This work provided a research foundation for connecting robotic sensing, mapping, and autonomous navigation with an educational lunar exploration experience. Together with our experience with the LEO rover at UNSA, it inspired us to translate advanced robotics concepts into interactive challenges for junior astronauts. Rover-Time adapts these ideas through virtual sensing and navigation; the experimental validation reported in the article applies to its research system, rather than constituting validation of our lunar simulator.


What factors did the team consider?

We considered clear instructions, progressive difficulty, readable interfaces, and a balance between engagement and scientific depth. Adapting language and challenges to younger learners remains a priority that requires continued user testing.

We also considered simulation performance, reuse of calculations, session synchronization, and progress preservation. On the scientific side, we paid attention to units, scale, data resolution, and source traceability.

Finally, we distinguish demonstrated prototype capabilities from future objectives. Ansys Rocky experiments provide supporting evidence, but their results are not automatically transferred into the game’s physics model. This transparency positions Rover-Time as an educational tool grounded in engineering, with a defined path toward stronger validation.
